title: Cardiopulmonary Physiotherapy
description: Respiratory assessment, airway clearance, physiotherapy in intensive care and surgery, pulmonary and cardiac rehabilitation.

topics.title: Respiratory Assessment
topics.summary: History, observation, auscultation, arterial blood gases, spirometry and chest imaging.

notes.b: Respiratory assessment records breathlessness (MRC dyspnoea scale 1–5), cough and sputum (volume, colour — purulent green/yellow suggests infection; frothy pink suggests pulmonary oedema; haemoptysis), wheeze, chest pain and smoking history (pack-years) or exposure to biomass smoke (common in Nigerian kitchens). Observation includes respiratory rate (normal adult 12–20/min), breathing pattern, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, clubbing and chest shape. Auscultation: vesicular breath sounds are normal; bronchial breathing suggests consolidation; wheeze indicates airway narrowing; crackles indicate secretions (coarse) or fibrosis/oedema (fine); reduced breath sounds suggest effusion, pneumothorax or collapse. Percussion: dull over consolidation/effusion, hyper-resonant with pneumothorax.

Arterial blood gases: normal pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 4.7–6.0 kPa (35–45 mmHg), PaO2 > 10.6 kPa (> 80 mmHg), HCO3 22–26 mmol/L. Type 1 respiratory failure: low PaO2 with normal/low PaCO2 (e.g. pneumonia); type 2: low PaO2 with high PaCO2 (ventilatory failure — e.g. COPD exacerbation, neuromuscular weakness). Pulse oximetry targets 94–98% (88–92% in patients at risk of CO2 retention). Spirometry: obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC < 0.7 — asthma, COPD) vs restrictive pattern (reduced FVC with normal or high ratio — fibrosis, chest wall deformity, neuromuscular disease). Chest X-ray identifies consolidation, collapse, effusion, pneumothorax and hyperinflation. Functional tests such as the 6-minute walk test measure exercise capacity.

topics.title: Airway Clearance and Breathing Techniques
topics.summary: ACBT, postural drainage, PEP devices, manual techniques, and breathing control.

notes.b: Airway clearance techniques help patients with excess secretions (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, pneumonia with retained secretions, post-TB bronchiectasis common in Nigeria). The active cycle of breathing techniques (ACBT) combines breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises (deep breaths with inspiratory hold) and the forced expiration technique (huffing). Gravity-assisted positioning (postural drainage) positions the affected lobe uppermost. Manual techniques include percussion (clapping) and vibrations/shaking during expiration. Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) and oscillating PEP devices (e.g. flutter) splint airways open. Autogenic drainage uses controlled breathing at different lung volumes. Contraindications/precautions include haemoptysis, unstable cardiovascular status, rib fractures, raised ICP, and osteoporosis (for percussion). Postural drainage head-down is avoided in reflux, raised ICP and recent surgery.

Breathing control (relaxed tidal breathing using the lower chest) reduces breathlessness and is used between more active techniques. Pursed-lip breathing slows expiration and prevents airway collapse in COPD. Positions of ease (forward lean sitting or standing with arms supported) relieve dyspnoea by optimising diaphragm length and accessory muscle use. Inspiratory muscle training uses threshold devices to strengthen weak inspiratory muscles. Incentive spirometry encourages sustained deep inspiration after surgery. Dysfunctional breathing (e.g. hyperventilation syndrome) is managed with breathing pattern retraining (e.g. Buteyko-type techniques in asthma).

topics.title: Physiotherapy in Intensive Care and Surgery
topics.summary: Mechanical ventilation basics, ICU physiotherapy, early mobilisation and postoperative care.

notes.b: ICU physiotherapists manage secretion retention, atelectasis and weakness in ventilated patients. Key concepts: modes of ventilation (volume- vs pressure-controlled, CPAP, PEEP — keeps alveoli open), FiO2, and weaning. Techniques include positioning (side-lying, head up 30–45° to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia), manual hyperinflation or ventilator hyperinflation, chest wall vibrations, and suctioning (pre-oxygenate, sterile technique, limit to about 10–15 seconds, suction on withdrawal). ICU-acquired weakness is common; early mobilisation (sitting over the bed edge, standing, walking, cycle ergometry) when stable reduces ventilator days and improves function. Always check vital signs, sedation (RASS), and safety criteria before and during treatment.

After upper abdominal and thoracic surgery, pain, anaesthesia and immobility reduce lung volumes (functional residual capacity) and impair cough, causing postoperative pulmonary complications (atelectasis, pneumonia). Preoperative education and inspiratory training reduce risk. Postoperative physiotherapy: adequate analgesia, early mobilisation (the most effective intervention), deep breathing exercises with inspiratory holds, supported coughing (wound support with a pillow or towel), incentive spirometry, and shoulder exercises after thoracic surgery. Chest drains: check for bubbling (air leak) and swinging (patency); never clamp without instruction. Cardiac surgery patients follow sternal precautions (limit pushing, pulling and lifting heavy loads with the arms for about 6–8 weeks).

topics.title: Pulmonary Rehabilitation
topics.summary: COPD, asthma, post-TB lung disease and components of pulmonary rehabilitation.

notes.b: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a comprehensive intervention for people with chronic respiratory disease (COPD, post-TB lung disease, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease). It includes supervised exercise training — aerobic (walking, cycling; about 30 minutes, 3 times per week, for 6–12 weeks), resistance training for upper and lower limbs — education (disease understanding, medication and inhaler technique, breathlessness management, exacerbation action plans, smoking cessation, nutrition), psychological support and energy conservation. Benefits include improved exercise capacity, reduced breathlessness, better quality of life and fewer hospital admissions. It is recommended for patients with MRC dyspnoea grade ≥ 3. Low-cost community programmes are feasible in Nigeria using walking and simple weights.
k: Improves capacity and quality of life

notes.b: Exercise intensity can be guided by the Borg breathlessness scale (aiming for moderate, e.g. 3–4 on the modified 0–10 scale) or perceived exertion. Oxygen supplementation during exercise may be needed for those who desaturate. In asthma, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is prevented with warm-up and pre-exercise bronchodilator; swimming is often well tolerated. Post-TB lung disease causes obstructive, restrictive or mixed defects and bronchiectasis — increasingly recognised in Nigeria. Inhaler technique education (spacers with metered-dose inhalers) is a key physiotherapy role. Patients should be taught to recognise exacerbations (increased breathlessness, sputum volume and purulence).

topics.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation
topics.summary: Phases of cardiac rehabilitation, exercise prescription, monitoring and heart failure.

notes.b: Cardiac rehabilitation supports recovery after myocardial infarction, coronary revascularisation (PCI, CABG), valve surgery and in stable heart failure. Phase I (inpatient): early mobilisation, education and discharge planning. Phase II (early outpatient, supervised, about 6–12 weeks): structured exercise with monitoring and risk-factor education. Phase III/IV (long-term maintenance): independent lifelong activity. Components: exercise training, risk-factor modification (smoking cessation, blood pressure, lipid and diabetes control, healthy diet, weight loss), psychosocial support and return to work/driving advice. Benefits include reduced cardiovascular mortality and readmissions and improved quality of life. With rising hypertension, diabetes and obesity, cardiac rehabilitation is increasingly needed in Nigeria.
k: Phase I inpatient; II supervised outpatient; III/IV maintenance

notes.b: Exercise prescription follows FITT: Frequency (most days), Intensity (moderate — 40–70% of heart rate reserve, Borg RPE 11–14 'somewhat hard'), Time (build to 20–60 minutes) and Type (aerobic — walking, cycling; plus resistance training). Include a 10–15 minute warm-up and cool-down. Beta-blockers blunt heart rate response, so RPE guides intensity. Stop exercise if chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, arrhythmias, or a fall in systolic BP occurs. The Karvonen formula: target HR = [(HRmax − HRrest) × intensity] + HRrest. In stable heart failure (NYHA I–III), exercise improves capacity and symptoms; avoid in decompensated failure. Hypertensive patients benefit from aerobic exercise, which lowers BP by about 5–8 mmHg; avoid heavy isometric straining (Valsalva).
k: Stop if chest pain or BP falls
